title: I allocated $3B to quant hedge funds for years. Now I'm trying to build one from scratch with AI tools, live, right now
author: stoaphil
selftext:
Some background: several years ago I was head PM at an allocator, picking and monitoring mostly quantitative hedge funds with about $3B under management. I'm a CFA charterholder. I've sat through hundreds of quant manager pitches, so I know what the good ones look like, and what gets hand-waved.

Now I'm testing how far one person with AI coding tools can get building a real systematic fund: data pipeline, signal research, backtesting that doesn't lie, risk and portfolio construction. No course, nothing to sell. I'm building it on stream and narrating how an allocator would pick it apart.

Even the stream itself is run by an AI agent (it runs OBS, health checks and the recording), which is its own rabbit hole.

Live now:  
Twitch: [twitch.tv/sudomyshkin](http://twitch.tv/sudomyshkin)  
YouTube: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DyV2zwFZDGw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DyV2zwFZDGw)

Questions welcome in chat, especially "that backtest is overfit" ones. Not investment advice, not raising money, just building in public.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
With AI coding tools, the number of signal variants tried could become an interesting part of the stream. A promising result after five attempts means something different from the winner of 500, including discarded variants nobody sees. I'd keep a running experiment log with the hypothesis, variants attempted, and why each was rejected.

From your experience allocating $3B to quant managers, what evidence would you require to distinguish a repeatable research process from a selectively presented backtest, and could you make that evidence visible as you build?

replies.author: stoaphil
replies.body:
"what evidence would you require to distinguish a repeatable research process from a selectively presented backtest" -- a lot... but most importantly capital at risk (even a little bit) to work out kinks  
"and could you make that evidence visible as you build" -- for sure

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the part the AI tools get wrong every time, in my experience, is the fill, not the signal. the code fills you at the bar's close on the same bar the signal fires, and nobody notices until paper trading disagrees with the backtest. worth making the stream's first "that's overfit" question about where the fill price comes from rather than the model.

Quantradin is the thing I built for this half of the problem: it backtests and paper trades a strategy using a real quoted fill when one exists and a modeled spread when it doesn't. costs nothing, trades paper only, easy to find by name if you want an outside opinion on the pipeline once the stream has one.

replies.author: stoaphil
replies.body: Very cool. I'm most likely going to be using Nautilus Trader rather than building my own execution stack.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: solid choice. its backtest engine has a real fill model with latency and slippage probability rather than close-of-bar fills, which is the exact thing most of the AI-written stacks skip.

replies.author: zopf
replies.body: I'm using NT as well, been testing on the 2.x RC and executing live. So far so good

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Re "I allocated $3B to quant hedge funds for years. Now I'm trying to build one from scratch with AI tools, live, right now":

The allocator-turned-builder angle is genuinely valuable content, most 'building a quant fund with AI' streams come from people who've never sat on the other side of a due diligence call, so knowing exactly what gets hand-waved in a pitch versus what's real should make the narration a lot sharper than the usual retail backtest showcase. On the 'backtest that doesn't lie' goal specifically, curious how you're planning to handle the meta-problem: you're an experienced allocator building this live, which means you already have priors about what a good result should look like, that's exactly the kind of implicit knowledge that leaks into parameter choices and creates a subtler overfitting problem than the naive kind, since it's coming from domain expertise rather than curve-fitting. Also interesting that even the stream infrastructure is AI-agent-run, that's its own reliability surface (OBS health checks, recording) separate from the actual research pipeline, worth flagging clearly to viewers which failures belong to which system when something breaks live.

Data pipeline and signal research is exactly the layer EventTrader's built around too, would be interesting to see how your event-driven signal sourcing compares if that comes up on stream. [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

replies.author: stoaphil
replies.body:
Great questions  
1. On "backtest that doesn't lie" -- backtests will always be overfit. You have to be honest during your research process and not do little parameter changes on a strategy until it works. If you have to do that more than 2-3 times then it probably isn't a good strategy.

2. Stream infra run by AI agent -- yeah feel free to drop in the stream and I can talk about it. I've been building an app called StreamBuddy which is just software purpose built for an AI to manage the stream on my behalf (so I don't have to square-peg-round-hole with legacy softwares).

I'll be streaming again today so feel free to drop by.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
The "2-3 tweaks max" heuristic is a good practical guardrail, though worth being precise with yourself about what counts as a tweak versus a redesign — swapping a parameter value is one thing, but changing the entry condition after seeing it fail is really starting a new hypothesis test, not iterating on the old one, even if it doesn't feel that way in the moment. Easy line to blur when you're the one who wants the result to work.

StreamBuddy's a fun rabbit hole on its own — curious whether it's just health-check/restart automation or if it's actually making judgment calls about stream state (when to cut to backtest results vs. commentary, etc.), since that's a different reliability bar than "keep OBS alive." Will drop by the stream.
